lead: An instrumentation amplifier is a difference amplifier with two buffered inputs. Two non-inverting buffers share one resistor R_G, so the differential input appears across R_G and the first stage gives a gain of 1 + 2R/R_G while passing the common-mode voltage at a gain of exactly 1. A second difference amplifier subtracts that common mode. Input resistance is 10⁹ Ω or more and equal on both sides, and CMRR above 100 dB is routine. Strain-gauge load cells in weighing scales, ECG and EEG front ends, thermocouples and shunt current sensing all use it.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the virtual short, 6.2 for the non-inverting gain 1 + R_f/R₁, and 6.3 for the difference amplifier and its resistor-matching limit.

sections.h3: Why one difference amplifier is not enough

blocks.text: The difference amplifier of 6.3 looks like the whole answer: two inputs, one output, common mode removed. Put it straight on a real sensor and two problems appear.

First, it loads the sensor. Each input shunts the source with about R₁ to ground. With R₁ = 10 kΩ and a source resistance of 100 kΩ the divider passes only about 9 % of the signal. Worse, if the two source resistances differ, the two dividers differ, so common-mode noise turns into a false differential signal.

Second, its CMRR is set by resistor tolerance, not by the op-amp. Cancellation needs R₁/R_f to match on both sides. Ordinary 1 % resistors leave roughly 50 dB of CMRR, and raising the gain does not help. A bridge sitting on a 2 V common mode with a 5 mV signal needs far better.

A bridge, a thermocouple or a skin electrode therefore asks for four things: input resistance above 10⁹ Ω, the same resistance on both inputs, gain set by one resistor, and CMRR above 100 dB. The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier gives all four.

A₁ and A₂ are non-inverting amplifiers. Each has a feedback resistor R from its output to its own inverting input. One resistor R_G joins the two inverting inputs. The inputs v₁ and v₂ go to the non-inverting inputs.
By the virtual short of 6.1, the inverting input of A₁ sits at v₁ and that of A₂ at v₂, so the whole difference v₁ − v₂ appears across R_G and the current through it is i = (v₁ − v₂)/R_G.

No current enters an op-amp input, so the same i flows through both R's. From the output of A₂ to the output of A₁ the path crosses R_G and two R's, so the voltage between the two outputs is i(R_G + 2R).

blocks.where: v_o1 and v_o2 are the two first-stage outputs in volts; v₁ and v₂ are the input voltages in volts; R is the feedback resistor of each buffer in ohms, equal on both sides; R_G is the gain resistor between the two inverting inputs in ohms.

blocks.text: Set v₁ = v₂ = v_cm. Then i = 0, no voltage drops across the R's, and both outputs sit at v_cm. The common-mode gain of this stage is exactly 1, fixed by the buffers and independent of resistor tolerance.
A₃, the difference amplifier of 6.3, takes the two outputs. Its differential gain is R_f/R₁ and its common-mode gain is near zero when its four resistors match. Multiply the stages:

blocks.where: A_d is the differential gain, a pure number; R and R_G are as above; R_f is the feedback resistor and R₁ the input resistor of the second stage, in ohms, matched on both sides.

blocks.text: The input resistance seen by the sensor is the op-amp input resistance, 10⁹ Ω to 10¹² Ω, the same on both inputs.

sections.h3: Gain, CMRR and where the errors come from

items: Gain setting: most designs fix the second stage at 1 (all four resistors equal) and use R_G as the only knob. For large gain A_d ≈ 2R/R_G, so a 1 % error in R_G gives about 1 % gain error. Use a 0.1 % metal-film resistor for R_G.

Design formula: invert the gain equation, R_G = 2R/(A_d R₁/R_f − 1). With A_d = 1000, R = 25 kΩ and a unity second stage, R_G is about 50 Ω — small enough that the resistance of the switch, socket and PCB track adds to it and spoils gain accuracy.

CMRR: the input stage passes the common mode at gain 1, so it does not limit the CMRR. The overall CMRR is set by the matching of the second-stage resistors, or in a monolithic part by their on-chip trimming: 100 dB to 120 dB at gain 10. Built from discrete op-amps, the second-stage resistors decide the CMRR however good the op-amps are.
Bandwidth: the closed-loop bandwidth is the op-amp gain-bandwidth product divided by A_d (see Unit 3), so gain 1000 on a 1 MHz op-amp leaves about 1 kHz.

Two-op-amp version: it saves one op-amp and two resistors, but its inputs are not alike. One is a high-resistance non-inverting input; the other is a resistor to a virtual node. Unequal source resistances then convert common mode into differential error.

sections.h3: Where it is used, and practical points

items: Strain-gauge bridge: four gauges on a beam inside a load cell give a few millivolts on top of a large common-mode level. The in-amp is the first block of a weighing scale.
ECG and EEG: skin electrodes have thousands of ohms of source resistance and pick up metres of 50 Hz mains coupling as common mode. The in-amp must not load the electrodes and must reject that mains.
Thermocouple: a few tens of microvolts on a slowly drifting common-mode voltage; the in-amp feeds the cold-junction correction and an ADC.
Shunt current sensing: a shunt of a fraction of an ohm carries the load current. The in-amp measures the small drop across it while both terminals swing with the motor supply.

Practical: keep the two input leads short, equal and twisted together. Drive the cable shield from the common-mode voltage — the midpoint of R_G if R_G is two equal halves, or the average of the two buffer outputs — so the shield moves with the common mode, not with the signal, and cable capacitance is not charged by the signal. Mount R_G close to the chip and return the bridge supply ground to one point.

figure.caption: The two buffers give a high and equal input resistance, R_G sets the first-stage gain, and the difference amplifier A₃ removes the common-mode voltage that both buffers passed through.

spec.title: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier
spec.aria: Two buffers with high input impedance feed a shared gain resistor R_G and a difference amplifier that removes the common-mode voltage.

examples.question: An instrumentation amplifier is built with R = 25 kΩ in each first-stage feedback path, R_G = 1 kΩ, and a second-stage difference amplifier in which all four resistors are 10 kΩ. The differential input is 5 mV riding on a common-mode voltage of 2 V, and the amplifier's CMRR is 100 dB. (a) Find the total differential gain. (b) Find the output caused by the differential part. (c) Find the output error caused by the 2 V common mode.
steps: Differential part of the output: 51 × 5 mV = 255 mV.
Output error from 2 V of common mode: 2 V × 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.02 mV, about 0.4 % of the 255 mV wanted signal.
examples.answer: The total gain is 51, the differential output is 255 mV, and the 2 V common mode adds only about 1.02 mV at the output.
examples.check:
R = 25e3
RG = 1e3
Rf = 10e3
R1 = 10e3
vd = 5e-3
vcm = 2.0
cmrr_db = 100
g1 = 1 + 2*R/RG
g2 = Rf/R1
ad = g1*g2
acm = ad/(10**(cmrr_db/20))
print(g1)
print(g2)
print(ad)
print(ad*vd*1e3)
print(acm)
print(acm*vcm*1e3)

traps: Writing the first-stage gain as 1 + R/R_G and losing the factor 2. There are two resistors R, one in each buffer's feedback path.
Blaming R_G for poor CMRR. R_G sets the gain; the CMRR is set by the matching of the second-stage resistors, or by the trimming inside a monolithic part.
Saying the input stage has zero common-mode gain. It has exactly 1; the whole common-mode voltage appears at both outputs and the difference amplifier removes it.
Adding the two stage gains instead of multiplying them. Gains in cascade multiply: A_d = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R_f/R₁).
Treating an instrumentation amplifier as just another difference amplifier. The difference is the buffered, equal, gigaohm input resistance and the CMRR above 100 dB.

quiz.q: What is the common-mode gain of the input stage (A₁ and A₂ with R_G) of a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier?
quiz.a: Exactly 1. With v₁ = v₂ no current flows in R_G, no voltage drops across the feedback resistors, and both outputs sit at the common-mode input voltage.

quiz.q: Which component sets the differential gain of the instrumentation amplifier, and which components set its CMRR?
quiz.a: R_G sets the gain, through 1 + 2R/R_G. The matching of the second-stage resistors R₁ and R_f sets the CMRR.

quiz.q: Explain why the whole differential input v₁ − v₂ appears across R_G in the input stage.
quiz.a: Each op-amp has negative feedback through R, so the virtual short holds: the inverting input of A₁ is at v₁ and that of A₂ is at v₂. R_G connects these two nodes directly, so the voltage across it is v₁ − v₂.

quiz.q: An instrumentation amplifier uses R = 49.4 kΩ in both first-stage feedback paths, R_G = 1 kΩ, and a second stage with all four resistors equal. Find the total differential gain.
quiz.a: First stage: 1 + 2(49.4 kΩ)/(1 kΩ) = 1 + 98.8 = 99.8. Second stage: all four resistors are equal, so R_f/R₁ = 1. Total A_d = 99.8 × 1 ≈ 100.

quiz.q: An instrumentation amplifier has a differential gain of 100 and a CMRR of 100 dB. A 1 V common-mode voltage appears at its input. Find the common-mode gain and the resulting output error.
quiz.a: CMRR ratio = 10^(100/20) = 10⁵. A_cm = 100/10⁵ = 10⁻³. Output error = 10⁻³ × 1 V = 1 mV.

quiz.q: You need a differential gain of 1000 from a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with R = 25 kΩ per buffer and a unity-gain second stage. Find R_G and state two practical problems with your answer.
quiz.a: R_G = 2R/(A_d − 1) = 50 kΩ/999 ≈ 50.05 Ω. Problems: (i) at about 50 Ω the resistance of the switch, socket and PCB track is a noticeable fraction of R_G, so the gain error is large and the tolerance of R_G passes straight into the gain; (ii) bandwidth falls to the op-amp gain-bandwidth product divided by 1000, so a 1 MHz op-amp gives about 1 kHz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Monolithic instrumentation amplifiers put all three op-amps and the trimmed second-stage resistors on one die, so a single external resistor sets the gain and the CMRR is a datasheet number rather than a design chore. Medical front ends add an isolation barrier and a right-leg drive amplifier that injects the inverted common mode back into the patient to cancel mains pickup. Search next for "current-sense amplifier" and "right-leg drive ECG".
